name: Race predictor
seoTitle: Race predictor Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Race predictor: work out predicted time from the run distance and the run time. A free sports calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Race predictor calculator turns the run distance, the run time and the new run distance into predicted time. That makes it useful for a training session, a performance comparison or a competition result. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Race predictor calculator work?
sections.html:
The Race predictor calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports predicted time in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the run distance, the run time and the new run distance.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

sections.title: The formula behind the Race predictor calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Predicted time=(run time × (new run distance ÷ run distance ^ 53 ÷ 50))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Run distance = 30 km, Run time = 10 hrs and New run distance = 30 km. Working through the relationship above gives Predicted time = 10 hrs.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Predicted time = 10 hrs should be roughly the size you expected from Run distance = 30 km and Run time = 10 hrs.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in hours / minutes / seconds, and convertible to any of the 27 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in kilometers
  • Time, opening in hours / minutes / seconds
  • Length, opening in kilometers
  • Time, opening in hours / minutes / seconds

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Race predictor calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Tracking progress across a training block
  • Planning a session around a target you already know
  • Comparing two athletes or two attempts fairly
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the run distance, the run time and the new run distance — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Race predictor calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The unit chips cover the units listed on the page. A historical or regional unit that is missing can still be used by converting it to a listed unit first.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — run distance for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Switch the units to the ones you normally use and confirm the numbers are unchanged apart from their label; if they are not, a chip was on the wrong setting.

faq.q: What does the Race predictor calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns predicted time, derived from the run distance, the run time and the new run distance. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Race predictor calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the run distance, the run time and the new run distance, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter run distance in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Run distance opens in kilometers and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Predicted time = 10 hrs. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Race predictor calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
